title: Houthis Strike Najran Airport and Aramco Facility as Saudi-Yemen Conflict Intensifies
excerpt: The latest drone attacks extend a month-long Houthi campaign targeting Saudi oil infrastructure, airports, and shipping lanes, raising concerns for millions of Indian workers in the Gulf.
body:
• Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed drone attacks on Najran airport and a Saudi Aramco facility in southern Saudi Arabia on Thursday, the latest in a series of strikes since late July.
  • The group has launched dozens of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, airports, and tankers since declaring a maritime embargo on Saudi shipping on July 20.
  • Saudi Arabia has responded by forging a joint defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan and launching a Red Sea maritime coalition to deter further escalation.
  • The conflict threatens stability for over 2.5 million Indian workers in the Gulf region and adds pressure to global energy markets that supply roughly 85 percent of India's crude oil imports.

The Latest Attacks

Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Thursday that they carried out two drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting what they described as a sensitive military target at Najran airport and a Saudi Aramco oil facility in the southern Najran region, according to the group's military spokesperson Yahya Saree. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities, Reuters reported.

The attacks mark at least the third time since late July that the Iran-aligned group has targeted Najran, a city near the Saudi-Yemeni border that has been a frequent flashpoint in the decade-long conflict. On August 4, the Houthis claimed a drone strike on what they called a sensitive target at Najran Airport, and on August 14, a separate drone attack struck an Aramco facility in the same region.

A Month-Long Escalation

The intensified campaign traces back to July 20, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, claiming it was a response to an alleged Saudi blockade of Houthi-held areas in Yemen — an allegation Riyadh has firmly denied.

Since then, the group has claimed a rapid series of attacks: drone strikes on Aramco oil facilities in Jizan and Yanbu on July 25, a ballistic missile attack on a Saudi oil tanker in the northern Red Sea in early August, and recurring strikes on Najran and other southern Saudi targets. On August 14, the Houthis also fired six ballistic missiles at the Red Sea port city of Mocha in government-held territory, killing at least four civilians, according to the Yemeni government.

Houthi claims have in the past been exaggerated, and Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the extent of damage from many of the reported strikes.

Saudi Arabia Builds a Web of Alliances

Riyadh has responded by assembling a network of defensive partnerships. Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan in Mecca, signaling a willingness to escalate if diplomatic options fail. The kingdom also launched joint airstrikes with the United States targeting Iraqi militias linked to attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure — the first publicly acknowledged Saudi military retaliation during the broader Iran-U.S. conflict.

"This is Saudi Arabia's way to signal to Iran that we are willing to go further up the ladder, of course first that of diplomacy before crossing the line of diplomacy to the other side."

— Yasmine Farouk, Crisis Group

Saudi Arabia also announced plans to lead a maritime defense coalition in the Red Sea, where Houthi attacks on shipping have disrupted one of the world's most critical trade corridors. The Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, handles roughly 12 percent of global seaborne trade.

Implications for Indian Workers and Energy Security

The escalation carries direct consequences for the Indian diaspora. Over 2.5 million Indian nationals live and work in Saudi Arabia and the broader Gulf states, forming one of the largest overseas Indian communities in the world. Previous rounds of Middle East conflict have prompted consular advisories and, in extreme cases, large-scale evacuation operations by the Indian government.

India's energy dependence adds another layer of concern. The country imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, with Saudi Arabia among its top three suppliers. Sustained attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure — particularly Aramco facilities that underpin a significant share of global crude output — could tighten supply and push prices higher, straining India's import bill and widening its current account deficit.

What Comes Next

The Houthi campaign shows no signs of easing. The group has repeatedly vowed to expand attacks until its demands regarding the alleged Saudi blockade are met. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces the difficult task of responding forcefully enough to deter further strikes without being pulled deeper into the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, the Houthis' primary backer.

Yemen has been mired in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led military coalition the following year. A 2022 UN-brokered truce brought a period of relative calm, but the recent escalation has shattered that fragile peace. For Riyadh, the question is no longer whether to respond, but how far to go.
nri_angle: Over 2.5 million Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia face heightened security concerns as Houthi attacks escalate, while India s heavy crude oil dependence on Saudi supplies adds energy market pressure.
author: Diaspora Desk
